The Architect of All Possible Cities

Jonathan Gibson stood in the pristine white chamber, his worn boots leaving faint dust marks on the crystalline floor. The massive architectural simulation engine dominated the center of the room, its holographic projectors shimmering with potential.

"Gibson," called Dr. Helena Vasquez, the lead temporal physicist, her voice echoing off the crystalline walls. "We've run the compatibility matrices three times. Your neural patterns show only minimal deviation under retro-temporal stress—far below the threshold that incapacitated our other candidates."

He stripped off his patched coveralls, as instructed in the preparation room, and stepped into the housing of the enormous mechanism. All around him, technicians in clean jumpsuits—the uniform of the privileged scientific caste—made their final adjustments.

On the observation platform above, the water barons sat in judgment. Tarek Stephens of the desalination monopoly. Rita Jenkins, the atmospheric moisture harvesting tycoon. Carmen Russell, the recycled water magnate. Their clothing bore patches too, but the patches matched their surrounding fabric—a luxury beyond imagination for someone like Gibson.

He knew what they saw when they looked at him: a maintenance worker from the North American Water Reclamation Facility in Unity, Veldoria. Someone who monitored filtration systems that processed precious water at about one-sixth of the pre-Drought capacity. Someone thoroughly content with the half-ration of purified water he received each payday.

What they didn't see was why he was here instead of any of the dozens of trained temporal specialists who had applied for this mission.

Director-General Lila Cole approached, her worn garments nearly as mismatched as those Gibson had removed. "Young man, you understand the fundamentals of the control panel? The blue valve mechanism?"

"I've studied the schematics for weeks, Director. The architectural principles aren't complicated—it's a standard hydraulic interface from that era."

"Yes, yes," Cole said, her head nodding tremulously. "Many of our specialists could operate such equipment. The operation itself is quite straightforward. It's the..." she trailed off, glancing at Vasquez.

The physicist stepped forward. "What the Director means is that the mechanical task itself requires no special training. A child could turn the valve. The challenge has always been maintaining cognitive function during temporal displacement."

Gibson thought of his family—his wife, his four children. The water barons had promised them a lifetime pension of a full liter each of clean water daily. Even if he didn't return, they would be provided for better than almost any other family on Earth.

"The Vasquez tests showed I'm resistant," Gibson said. "That's enough for me."

"More than resistant," Vasquez corrected. "You maintained full consciousness during a thirty-second displacement that rendered Commander Okafor comatose for three days. We've traced your genealogical records extensively, searching for any factor that might explain—"

"Proceed," Carmen Russell commanded from the platform. "We didn't invest our resources to hear lectures."

Cole flinched but continued. "You will project back one hundred and thirteen years to June 15, 1976. The Ravenswood Dam Project in Thandor. You will turn the blue valve clockwise, preventing the cascading water management failure that caused the Drought."

She pressed a sealed data cube into his hands. "The AI specialists have suggested this precaution. Release it into the temporal medium just before materialization. If anything unexpected occurs, return immediately."

"He understands," Jenkins snapped. "Gibson. Move!"

Jonathan Gibson darted to the rear of the machine and pressed the activation sequence.

*flick!*

"Good old Maria Gibson," Jon Gibson laughed as he looked at the concerned faces of his two colleagues.

Stephen Porter and Jordan Hughes had constructed the compact simulation engine with him in this secret laboratory under the water reclamation facility. They were equally eager to go, but the displacement tests had shown only Jon could maintain consciousness for the required duration.

He squeezed into the housing of the intricate mechanism, barely glancing at the miniature holographic projectors he'd helped build. This machine was the last hope of 2089, even if the world didn't know of its existence and would try to prevent its operation.

"You're certain you can manage the controls?" Hughes asked for the dozenth time.

"Jordan, the dam interface is elementary. Any first-year architecture student could operate it. That was never the concern."

"No," Porter agreed, his pudgy face serious. "The concern was finding someone who wouldn't fall unconscious mid-displacement and materialize half-embedded in a concrete wall."

In their cautious, protective, life-preserving world, the population had dwindled to fewer than a hundred thousand—well below the danger point where a species might be eliminated by a new catastrophe. The Plague had seen to that, sterilizing most and leaving the rest barely capable of reproduction. Jon Gibson, with his three children, was almost unknown in his fertility.

Everyone on Earth was engaged in some form of scientific research—physical labor had long been performed by robots. The government ensured ample supplies of goods and asked only that citizens experiment without risk to their own lives. Every human being was a much-prized, highly protected rarity.

"Be cautious, Jon," Porter said, handing him a small metal container. "When you go back and turn that blue valve counterclockwise—causing the cascading failure instead of letting it function properly—you'll create a new world. Maybe they'll get the same idea and try to change things back. This container holds a document explaining why ours is the worst possible future."

"What do I do with it?"

"Push it into the temporal medium a moment before you materialize. That medium exists independent of all possible futures. My hypothesis is that something immersed in it won't be altered by a new time sequence."

Hughes gripped Jon's shoulder. "Any time you feel like taking an unnecessary risk, remember that Stephen and I will stand trial if you don't return. We might lose professional status and spend our lives supervising water filtration robots."

"I know this is a first experiment," Gibson said. "If anything unexpected appears, I'll come back for advice."

He reached for the control that activated the simulation engine.

*flick!*

The dense gray murk surrounded Jonathan Gibson's machine. According to his instruments, he was in 1976. He drifted backward to June 15th, watching the indicator approach the crucial moment.

He stopped the machine completely.

All he had to do now was materialize and turn the blue valve toward him. But wasn't there something he was supposed to do first?

He picked up the sealed data cube and tossed it into the murk. A solid object floating near the entrance caught his eye. He extended his arm—it was cold!—and pulled it inside.

A small metal container. Curiously, he opened it.

The document inside described a different world—one where the dam had functioned properly and something called "Anderson's Syndrome" had devastated human fertility instead of the Drought destroying the water supply. A world of abundance but extinction through sterility rather than thirst.

Jonathan Gibson finished reading and sighed. What a wonderful world that would be! What a comfortable place to live!

He began materializing at the crucial moment.

*flick!*

The soupy gray murk surrounded Jon Gibson's machine. According to the insulated register, he was in 1976. He maneuvered slowly backward to June 15th, watching the register approach the crucial moment.

He froze the machine in place.

All he had to do now was materialize and push the blue valve away from him. But he was supposed to do something first.

He dropped the metal container into the murk. A solid object floating near the opening attracted his attention. He pulled the sealed data cube inside.

The document described a different world—one where the dam had malfunctioned and cascading water failure had caused global drought instead of the Plague destroying human fertility. A world of scarcity and water barons rather than safety and sterility.

Jon Gibson finished reading and sighed. What an exciting place that would be! What a dynamic world!

He began materializing at the crucial moment.

*flick!*

As the control center materialized around him, Jonathan Gibson felt fear at what he was doing. The Director-General had warned him to return if anything unusual appeared.

But in this other world, this other 2089 with its abundance of water and protection of every life, a man with four children would be important—maybe the most important on Earth! Robots would work for him. The state would treasure his offspring.

This other world had troubles, but it was much nicer than where he'd come from. The fear left him, and for the first time in his life, Jonathan Gibson felt power.

He saw the blue valve pointing upward. The valve controlling the dam.

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

As the control center oscillated into reality around him, Jon Gibson felt shame. He'd promised Stephen and Jordan to abandon the experiment if a new factor appeared.

But in this other world, this other 2089 with its chaos and opportunity, someone like himself would be a monarch of the water market. A lord making his own rules. So what if the weak suffered?

The document's fools hadn't even grasped that an alternate time track meant their own non-existence. His world was moribund; this alternate was fighting destiny. It deserved a chance.

He saw the blue valve pointing downward. The valve controlling the dam.

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

... pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... toward him.

*flick!*

... away from him.

*flick!*
